items.title: Exactly which numbers are rational?
items.student: Classify these exact numbers as rational or irrational and justify: −3;0;2/5;0.125;0.333… with 3 repeating forever;√9;√2;π. State whether each is also an integer. Give a fraction for every rational number and explain why a finite calculator display alone cannot classify an exact number. Diagnostic: evaluate −4+7 and 3/4+1/2. Integers include negative whole numbers, zero and positive whole numbers.
items.teacher: Rational:−3=−3/1,0=0/1,2/5,0.125=1/8,0.333…=1/3,√9=3=3/1. Integer members:−3,0,√9. Irrational:√2 andπ. A rational number is expressible as a/b for integers a,b with b≠0. Irrational real numbers cannot be expressed that way. A terminating or eventually repeating decimal is rational. A rounded display is an approximation, not an exact expansion. Diagnostic answers 3 and 5/4. Do not classify every radical as irrational.

items.title: Decimal claims and exact values
items.student: Card A says “π=3.14 exactly”. Card B says “√2 is rational because my calculator displays 1.414213562”. Card C says “√16 is irrational because it has a root sign”. Correct each claim. Place−3,−1/2,0,√2,2 on a number line. Use 1.4² and 1.5² to bracket√2. Compare the exact value 1/3 with a display 0.333333333: what is exact, what is approximate? Write two different exact numbers whose rounded display to 2 decimal places is 1.41.
items.teacher: π≈3.14, not exact equality. A finite rounded display does not make√2 rational; √2 is irrational. √16=4 is rational. Number-line order as listed.1.4²=1.96<2<2.25=1.5², so 1.4<√2<1.5.1/3 is exact;0.333333333 is a terminating rational approximation if treated as written. Examples 1.411 and 1.414 both round to 1.41. Use ≈ for rounded results. The bracketing task locates√2, not a proof of irrationality.

items.title: Signed and fractional operations
items.student: Work with exact fractions: (a)−3/4+5/6; (b)2/3−5/4; (c)(−2/3)×(9/4); (d)(3/5)÷(−9/10). For each show intermediate working and one check. Error analysis: A learner claims(−2)×(−5)=−10 and 3/4+1/2=4/6. Correct both explanations. Explain what division by zero would require and why it is not defined in the real numbers.
items.teacher: (a)(−9+10)/12=1/12; (b)(8−15)/12=−7/12; (c)−18/12=−3/2; (d)(3/5)×(−10/9)=−2/3. Possible checks: reverse operation, equivalent fractions, sign/magnitude estimate. (−2)×(−5)=10; common denominators are needed for addition, giving 5/4. Division a÷0 would require a unique x with 0 x=a: no solution if a≠0 and no unique solution if a=0. Never turn an error display into a numeric result.

items.title: Combined operations and grouping
items.student: Evaluate with working: A=3/4−[1/2÷(−2)]; B=(−3)²−2(5−8); C=6÷3×2; D=−3². State why B starts with 9 while D starts with−9. A learner enters 3/4−1/2÷−2 on a calculator without grouping: write an unambiguous bracketed entry and verify with exact arithmetic. Create one expression using rational numbers and parentheses whose value is 1/2; exchange and check it.
items.teacher: A=3/4−(−1/4)=1. B=9−2(−3)=15. C=(6÷3)×2=4 because multiplication/division have equal priority and are processed left to right. D=−(3²)=−9; parentheses determine whether the negative sign is part of the base. Correct entry can be(3÷4)−((1÷2)÷(−2)); input method varies by calculator. Example expression 1−(3/4−1/4)=1/2. Do not teach that multiplication always precedes division.

items.title: Reciprocals, calculator limits and zero
items.student: For each exact nonzero number find its reciprocal:4;−5;3/4;−0.2;√2. Give an exact form where possible and a decimal approximation to 3 decimal places. Verify each product with its original value. Explain why 0 has no reciprocal. A calculator shows 0.707106781 for 1/√2: is that the exact reciprocal? Record the model/key sequence you used; if calculators are shared, each learner must make and record at least one entry.
items.teacher: Reciprocals:1/4=0.250;−1/5=−0.200;4/3≈1.333;−5=−5.000;1/√2=√2/2≈0.707. Exact products equal 1; products using rounded values may differ slightly.0 r cannot equal 1, so zero has no reciprocal. A calculator display is approximate for the irrational reciprocal. The reciprocal of a negative number is negative. Prepare basic scientific calculators for roots; if unavailable, supply √2≈1.414213562 and make calculator use a scheduled accessible station. A printed calculation is not evidence that a learner can operate the calculator.

items.title: Interpret a rational-number model
items.student: Fictional contexts; no personal measurements.1 A tank contains 3/4 L of clean water.1/6 L is used and then 1/3 L added. Find the final amount.2 A credit balance of KES50 is changed by a debit of KES80 and a credit of KES45. Find the balance using signed numbers.3 A fictional record lists body temperatures 36.8°C and 37.4°C. Copy them with units and calculate the signed change only; do not interpret health status. Recording note: a fictional blood-pressure entry 120/80 mmHg contains two readings, not an instruction to divide 120 by 80. Copy it into separate systolic/diastolic columns with units. Source for the two-number/unit convention: MedlinePlus, Measuring Blood Pressure, https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/measuring-blood-pressure/ (checked 13 November 2026). No personal measurements or medical advice are part of this task.4 A bottle holds 3/4 L. How many such bottles equal a total volume of 3 L? Explain the reciprocal’s role. State one assumption in each model.
items.teacher: 1.3/4−1/6+1/3=11/12 L; assume exact amounts/no loss beyond stated use.2.50−80+45=15 KES; assume no fees.3.37.4−36.8=0.6°C increase; this arithmetic alone does not establish health status. Blood-pressure recording columns: systolic 120 mmHg,diastolic 80 mmHg; the slash separates readings, not a fraction calculation. Reinforce accurate/private records; use fictional data only.4.3÷(3/4)=3×4/3=4 bottles; assume identical capacities and fully filled bottles. The reciprocal 4/3 has bottles per litre in this model, while 3/4 is litres per bottle. Arithmetic alone does not establish an actual temperature’s health significance; no clinical interpretation is taught.

items.title: Check and communicate a practical calculation
items.student: Fictional club plan: available liquid 2.5 L; reserve 1/4 L; each full serving 3/8 L. A poster promises 7 full servings. Calculate usable volume and the number of full servings possible. Explain the units and assumption of no spills. A peer says “2.25÷0.375=0.844”; diagnose a likely operation error and show a check. Add a short explanation of why exact rational-number reasoning is useful, and one appropriate calculator-care or respectful turn-taking action. This is a paper planning case, not food distribution.
items.teacher: 2.5−0.25=2.25 L=9/4 L; (9/4)÷(3/8)=6 servings exactly. Seven require 21/8 L=2.625 L before reserve, exceeding usable volume.0.844 is the rounded product 2.25×0.375=0.84375, not the quotient; multiplication by reciprocal 8/3 gives 6. Check 6×3/8=9/4 L. A reasoned usefulness statement should connect a decision to quantities/units and a verifiable check. Formative observation of device care/turn-taking is separate from the final numeric rubric.

items.title: Independent exact-number and context sheet
items.student: Use these new exact values and fictional data only. Classification list:0;−7/4;0.272727… with 27 repeating forever;√25;√3. A container holds 5/6 L;1/4 L is used and 1/3 L added. A credit balance KES−20 receives KES65 then a KES18 debit. A full portion is 2/5 L. A calculator may be used, but show exact working where requested. No fees, spills or volume changes beyond those stated. This sheet contains data only; use the separate final task prompts.
items.teacher: Release only for Lesson 8. Rational 0,−7/4, repeating decimal=27/99=3/11,√25=5; √3 irrational. Final container 11/12 L. Final balance 27 KES. Reciprocal 2/5 is 5/2=2.5. Exact reciprocal√3=1/√3≈0.577. Final arithmetic tasks and rubric are in the separate key. No teaching-card worked examples should accompany the independent sheet.
